warmup.q: A processor writes private var first: Box? = null into a generated file in package movemate.van. Box is declared in package movemate of the same module. What happens when the build compiles the generated file?
options: It compiles: generated code can see every class in the module
It fails with Unresolved reference 'Box': a generated file needs imports like any other file
KSP refuses to write the file, with an error from [ksp]
It compiles with a warning about a missing import
warmup.why: A generated file is ordinary source code, compiled together with yours, so it follows the same rules: a type from another package needs an import or its full name. KSP doesn't check generated code at all; the error comes from the Kotlin compiler afterwards, as e: LoadBuilder.kt:4:24 Unresolved reference 'Box'. The first option is tempting because both files live in one module, but a module is not a package.

opening:
A family is packing for a move. Every box is sealed, and its label lists what's inside. In this track your source files are those boxes. A KSP processor is a helper with a clipboard: it reads the labels and writes new cards that travel with the move. In the last lesson, the helper learned to copy a label out neatly, Lamp(name: String, bulbs: Int, shade: String?), for a person to read.

Today the card has a stricter reader. We'll generate a builder for each class: a small class that collects an object's values one call at a time and then builds it, LampBuilder().name("desk lamp").bulbs(1).shade(null).build(). Its reader is the Kotlin compiler, which has never once forgiven a missing import. Lesson 2 wrote its cards with a string template, text with values pasted in, so we'll start there. It works for Lamp, and then three of four ordinary classes fail to compile.

In this lesson, we'll watch that happen, swap the handwriting for a label printer called KotlinPoet, and read what it prints. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a handwritten builder that worked for Lamp and broke on four ordinary classes. A label printer fixed each slip: imports from %T, honest nullable types from toTypeName() and copy(nullable = true), Kitchen.Drawer from toClassName(), and backticks from %N.

In a processor of your own, search for a $ inside a string that becomes generated code. Each one marks a place where a type or a name should be a placeholder.

Next, we'll feed the builder classes it can't build, an interface, an object and a private constructor, and teach it to say so on the exact file and line. What should a processor do when the label is wrong?

sections.h: A builder from a string template, and four classes that break it
sections.html:
First, the job. MoveMate is the small app this track builds for the family's move. One of its classes is data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?), marked with the annotation @Builder. An annotation is the sticky note on the box: here it says "make a builder for this one". For each class with that note, our processor should write LampBuilder. It needs one private field per constructor parameter, each starting empty, and one setter per field that returns the builder, so that calls chain. Last comes build(), which calls Lamp's constructor.

The quickest way to write that file is lesson 2's way. Build the text line by line, then hand it to KSP's CodeGenerator, the object that creates new files. Java has had annotation processors, programs that run inside the compiler and write new source files, since Java 6. KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code, and faster than running Java's processors on Kotlin through kapt. Here is the heart of the template version, next to its closest Java equivalent:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor that writes text through the Filer
JavaFileObject file = processingEnv.getFiler().createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "Builder", type);
try (Writer out = file.openWriter()) {
    out.write("package " + pkg + ";\n\n");
    out.write("public class " + name + "Builder {\n");
    for (VariableElement p : params) {
        out.write("    private " + p.asType() + " " + p.getSimpleName() + ";\n");
    }
    // ... the setters and build(), line by line
    out.write("}\n");
}
Kotlin
// Naive: a builder from a string template
val text = buildString {
    appendLine("package $pkg")
    appendLine()
    appendLine("class ${name}Builder {")
    for (p in params) {
        appendLine("    private var ${p.name!!.asString()}: ${p.type.resolve()}? = null")
    }
    // ... the setters and build(), line by line
    appendLine("}")
}
codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(false, cls.containingFile!!), pkg, "${name}Builder")
    .use { it.write(text.toByteArray()) }

p.type.resolve() turns the type as written into a KSType, and pasting a KSType into a string prints its name. For Lamp, the result compiles and the builder works. It has one smudge: shade is already String?, the template adds its own ?, and the field comes out as String??. The compiler lets it through with a sigh, w: LampBuilder.kt:6:31 Redundant '?'.

Now four ordinary classes, each compiled on its own. The Try it below printed:

=== a type from another package: COMPILATION_ERROR
e: LoadBuilder.kt:4:24 Unresolved reference 'Box'.
=== a nullable list of nullable boxes: OK
w: ShelfBuilder.kt:4:35 Redundant '?'.
=== a nested class: COMPILATION_ERROR
e: DrawerBuilder.kt:9:18 Unresolved reference 'Drawer'.
=== a property named in: COMPILATION_ERROR
e: CrateBuilder.kt:4:17 Syntax error: Expecting property name or receiver type.
... and 11 more

Look at the shape of those lines: a file, a line and a column, and no [ksp]. KSP wrote all five files without a word. The Kotlin compiler found the problems afterwards, because a generated file is compiled exactly like one of yours.

That explains every failure. Load lives in package movemate.van and uses movemate.Box, so LoadBuilder.kt needs import movemate.Box, and the template wrote no imports at all. A KSType prints a short display name, Box or List<Box?>?, which reads well but is not promised to be valid source in another file. Drawer is nested inside Kitchen, so from outside its name is Kitchen.Drawer. And in is a hard keyword: a property may be called in only when it's written with backticks, `in`.

In the moving-house picture, the template is handwriting on the card. It abbreviates without saying what the abbreviation means (no import) and smudges a mark (??). It forgets which room a box sits in (Kitchen), and it writes a word the reader takes for an instruction (in).

You could fix each slip by hand: qualified names everywhere, a list of keywords to escape, a check before every ?. Each fix is fair, and together they add up to a small program that prints Kotlin code.

Generated code is ordinary source code. Print it with a tool that knows Kotlin.

That tool already exists, and it's called KotlinPoet.

try.title: Watch the template break
steps: Open labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l04/demo/TemplateBuilderDemo.kt and read TemplateBuilderProcessor at the top. It writes the builder as text, one appendLine at a time.
Predict which of the five cases will compile. Then run it from labs/: ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l04.demo.TemplateBuilderDemoKt.
Add a sixth case to cases: a Bag.kt in package movemate holding @Builder class Bag(val items: Map<String, List<Box>>) (copy the import from the Shelf case). Predict, then run again.
try.expect: The demo prints each generated file, then the compiler's first lines about it. Lamp and Shelf compile, each with Redundant '?'. Load, Drawer and Crate fail with the errors in this section; Crate alone gets 14. The Bag case compiles: every name in Map<String, List<Box>> happens to be visible from package movemate without an import. A template fails only on some inputs, which is why it so often passes the first test you write. On a busy machine the run takes 10 to 30 seconds, most of it the first compilation in memory.

sections.h: KotlinPoet builds the file from specs and four placeholders
sections.html:
KotlinPoet is a library from Square, here in version 2.4.0, that writes Kotlin source files from objects instead of strings. You describe what the file holds, such as a class with these properties and these functions. KotlinPoet prints it, with the imports, the indentation and the escaping done for you. In the picture, it's the label printer that replaces handwriting.

Each piece of code has its own description, called a spec. FileSpec describes a whole file, TypeSpec a class, PropertySpec a property, FunSpec a function, and ParameterSpec a parameter. You make each one with its builder and finish it with build(). Here is the smallest useful spec, one function, in both libraries:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: JavaPoet, KotlinPoet's older sibling for Java
MethodSpec greet = MethodSpec.methodBuilder("greet")
        .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC)
        .returns(String.class)
        .addStatement("return $S", "Hello from Lamp")
        .build();
// prints:  public String greet() {
//            return "Hello from Lamp";
//          }
Kotlin
val greet = FunSpec.builder("greet")
    .returns(STRING)
    .addStatement("return %S", "Hello from Lamp")
    .build()
// prints:  public fun greet(): kotlin.String = "Hello from Lamp"

KotlinPoet's single line of output shows three habits. KotlinPoet writes public itself; its docs say it generates "explicit visibility modifiers" to maximize portability. It turned a body of one return into an expression body. And printed on its own, a spec spells out kotlin.String. Inside a FileSpec, the same type prints as String, with import kotlin.String at the top of the file.

The string "return %S" is a format string: code text with placeholders, which KotlinPoet fills from the arguments that follow it. Four placeholders do nearly all the work in this lesson:

Placeholder Takes Prints
%T a type: ClassName, TypeName its name, and adds the import
%N a name: a string or a spec the name, with backticks if it needs them
%S a string a string literal, quoted, with " and $ escaped
%L anything the value as it is, with no escaping

%S given Write $room on each "fragile" box prints "Write ${'$'}room on each \"fragile\" box", which is the same text as a Kotlin string, $ and all. %L would paste it raw and break the file, and an unescaped $room would quietly read a variable named room. Each placeholder knows the one rule its kind of value needs, which is exactly what the handwriting kept forgetting.

Pass types with %T and names with %N. Never paste them into the format string.

The figure shows the whole builder as specs: five calls on the left, the part of LampBuilder.kt each one prints on the right. KotlinPoet, though, speaks in ClassName and TypeName, while our processor holds KSP symbols. The next step joins the two.

aside.title: Is there a JavaPoet for Java processors?
aside.html: Yes, and it came first. Square's JavaPoet is the original, and its README says it has been deprecated since 2020-10-10; it points users to Palantir's fork, package com.palantir.javapoet, whose latest release is 0.23.0. The shapes match KotlinPoet's (TypeSpec, MethodSpec, FieldSpec, JavaFile) with $ instead of % in format strings: $T, $N, $S, $L. JavaFile.writeTo(filer) passes the originating elements to javac's Filer, the same job writeTo(codeGenerator, ...) does for KSP. The Java twins in this lesson use those names.

sections.h: kotlinpoet-ksp turns KSP symbols into KotlinPoet names
sections.html:
kotlinpoet-ksp is KotlinPoet's small companion for processors, also version 2.4.0. It adds extension functions that turn KSP symbols into KotlinPoet names, and a writeTo that hands a finished file to KSP. The builder processor uses four of them.

cls.toClassName() turns a KSClassDeclaration, the symbol for a class, into a ClassName: a package plus one or more simple names. For the nested drawer that's package movemate with the names Kitchen and Drawer, and %T prints Kitchen.Drawer. String surgery on movemate.Kitchen.Drawer can't tell you whether Kitchen is a package or a class. ClassName knows. The builder's own name comes from the same parts, simpleNames.joinToString("") plus Builder, so the drawer gets KitchenDrawerBuilder.

param.type.toTypeName() turns a KSTypeReference, the type as written in the source, into a TypeName, with every type argument and every ? in place: List<Box?>?. To do that it resolves the type, the step lesson 3 called expensive, and if the type can't be resolved it throws (lesson 5 deals with that). The field needs the same type made nullable, and copy(nullable = true) does it without doubling anything: String becomes String?, and String? stays String?. That's the smudge from the template, gone.

Here is the setter in both languages:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor with JavaPoet
MethodSpec setterMethod(VariableElement param, ClassName builder) {
    String name = param.getSimpleName().toString();
    return MethodSpec.methodBuilder(name)
            .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC)
            .addParameter(TypeName.get(param.asType()), name)
            .returns(builder)
            .addStatement("this.$N = $N", name, name)
            .addStatement("return this")
            .build();
}
Kotlin
fun setterFunction(param: KSValueParameter, builder: ClassName): FunSpec {
    val name = nameOf(param)
    return FunSpec.builder(name)
        .addParameter(name, param.type.toTypeName())
        .returns(builder)
        .addStatement("this.%N = %N", name, name)
        .addStatement("return this")
        .build()
}

Read the Kotlin version aloud: a function named after the parameter, taking one parameter with the same name and type, and returning the builder. Its body sets the field and returns this. Both names go through %N, so in comes out as `in` in all three places.

The last two calls hand the file to KSP:

Java
// javac: the class is the originating element, and the Filer writes the file
TypeSpec builderType = TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder)
        // ... fields, setters, build()
        .addOriginatingElement(type)
        .build();
JavaFile.builder(packageName, builderType).build().writeTo(processingEnv.getFiler());
Kotlin
// KSP: the class's source file is the originating file, and writeTo hands it to the CodeGenerator
val builderType = TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder)
    // ... properties, setters, build()
    .addOriginatingKSFile(cls.containingFile!!)
    .build()
FileSpec.builder(builder).addType(builderType).build().writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false)

The originating file is the source file an output was made from, here Lamp.kt. aggregating = false says that this output depends on its originating files and nothing else. Together they are KotlinPoet's way of writing lesson 2's Dependencies(false, file): writeTo collects the originating files from the file's top-level specs and builds the Dependencies itself. aggregating has no default, so you decide every time. A wrong decision doesn't show on a clean build or in a test. It shows later, after an ordinary edit, as a generated file that has quietly disappeared. Lesson 7 makes that happen on purpose.

In the picture, the originating file is the note clipped to each card that says which box it came from. When that box is repacked next weekend, the helper knows exactly which card to redo.

Our processor is complete. Let's run it in a real build and read what it wrote.

The Java version calls .in("hall") and .object("mirror") with no backticks, because neither word is a keyword in Java.

sections.h: Reading the generated builder aloud, and where it stops
sections.html:
Here is LampBuilder.kt exactly as the lab's processor writes it, next to the builder a Java developer would write for a Java Lamp:

Java
// The same builder for a Java record Lamp(String name, int bulbs, String shade)
public class LampBuilder {
  private String name;
  private Integer bulbs;
  private String shade;

  public LampBuilder name(String name) {
    this.name = name;
    return this;
  }

  // bulbs(...) and shade(...) have the same shape

  public Lamp build() {
    if (name == null) throw new IllegalStateException("LampBuilder: name was not set");
    if (bulbs == null) throw new IllegalStateException("LampBuilder: bulbs was not set");
    return new Lamp(name, bulbs, shade);
  }
}
Kotlin
// Generated by BuilderProcessor from Lamp. Do not edit.
package movemate

import kotlin.Int
import kotlin.String

public class LampBuilder {
  private var name: String? = null

  private var bulbs: Int? = null

  private var shade: String? = null

  public fun name(name: String): LampBuilder {
    this.name = name
    return this
  }

  public fun bulbs(bulbs: Int): LampBuilder {
    this.bulbs = bulbs
    return this
  }

  public fun shade(shade: String?): LampBuilder {
    this.shade = shade
    return this
  }

  public fun build(): Lamp = Lamp(
    name = name ?: error("LampBuilder: name was not set"),
    bulbs = bulbs ?: error("LampBuilder: bulbs was not set"),
    shade = shade,
  )
}

Read it from the top. The file says where it came from and which package it's in, then imports kotlin.Int and kotlin.String, which KotlinPoet always writes although Kotlin would find them anyway. LampBuilder holds three empty slots. Each setter fills one slot and hands the builder back, so the calls chain. build() calls Lamp with named arguments. A slot that must be filled either has a value or stops the program with a message that names the builder and the slot. shade, which may be null, goes in as it is. The two-space indent and the blank line between members are KotlinPoet's house style, which is why the lab's first test compares the whole text.

Is it worth a library? The template's text took 23 lines and got one of five cases clean. The KotlinPoet functions take 48 lines, twice as many, and get all five right, plus the Bag and fun cases from the Try its. The gain isn't fewer lines. It's the cases you never had to think of.

Now the limits. KotlinPoet models declarations, not expressions. Its docs put it plainly: "the body of methods and constructors is not modeled." A body is a format string such as "%N = %N ?: error(%S),\n". KotlinPoet checks the names and types you pass in, and nothing about what the code means. If build() passed the arguments in the wrong order, KotlinPoet would print it faithfully and the compiler would object. That's why every test in this lesson's lab compiles the generated code and calls it.

This is also where the picture breaks. A label printer prints exactly the words you type. KotlinPoet edits as it prints: it adds imports, public and backticks, and turns a one-line return into an expression body. So read its output at least once before you trust it.

The second limit is KSP's, and our builder inherits it. Lesson 3 showed that a parameter's hasDefault says that a default exists, never what it is. So PlantBuilder can't fill in waterEveryDays = 7, and it asks you instead: PlantBuilder().kind("fern").potLitres(2.5).build() stops with PlantBuilder: waterEveryDays was not set. The label says "spare bulb included", and the helper can't open the box to see which bulb.

KotlinPoet checks the shape of the code, not its meaning. Compile and call what you generate.

There's one thing this builder can't do yet: say no. Give it an interface, and the !! in constructorParameters is waiting for it.

compare.title: The builder class, assembled with JavaPoet and with KotlinPoet

java.title: BuilderProcessor.java (javac, JavaPoet)
java.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor with JavaPoet TypeSpec builderType(TypeElement type, List<? extends VariableElement> params) { String pkg = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getPackageOf(type).getQualifiedName().toString(); ClassName builder = ClassName.get(pkg, type.getSimpleName() + "Builder"); TypeSpec.Builder spec = TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder).addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC); for (VariableElement p : params) { TypeName empty = TypeName.get(p.asType()).box(); // int becomes Integer, which can be null spec.addField(FieldSpec.builder(empty, p.getSimpleName().toString(), Modifier.PRIVATE).build()); spec.addMethod(setterMethod(p, builder)); } return spec.addMethod(buildMethod(type, params, builder)) .addOriginatingElement(type) .build(); } // then: JavaFile.builder(pkg, builderType(type, params)).build().writeTo(processingEnv.getFiler());

kotlin.title: BuilderProcessor.kt (KSP, KotlinPoet)
kotlin.html: fun builderType(cls: KSClassDeclaration): TypeSpec { val builder = builderName(cls) val params = constructorParameters(cls) return TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder) .addProperties(params.map(::builderProperty)) // private var name: String? = null .addFunctions(params.map { setterFunction(it, builder) }) .addFunction(buildFunction(cls, builder)) .addOriginatingKSFile(cls.containingFile!!) .build() } // then: builderFile(cls).writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false)

compare.note: The plan is the same call for call: a class, one field and one setter per parameter, build(), and the input the output came from. Three differences matter. JavaPoet needs addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC), while KotlinPoet writes public itself. To let a Java field start empty, box() turns int into Integer; Kotlin says the same with copy(nullable = true), and its TypeName keeps the ? right on every type argument too. And the originating input differs in size: javac's Filer takes elements (the class), KSP takes files (Lamp.kt). Gradle's incremental Java processing sorts whole processors into isolating and aggregating, while KSP decides per output, which lesson 7 takes apart.

steps.say: A user of LampBuilder asks for the other direction: start from an existing Lamp, change one value, build again. Start, as always, from the text you want KotlinPoet to print.
steps.code: public fun Lamp.toBuilder(): LampBuilder = LampBuilder().name(name).bulbs(bulbs).shade(shade) // in use: copy a lamp with two bulbs val brighter = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null).toBuilder().bulbs(2).build()

alt.html: public static LampBuilder toBuilder(Lamp lamp) { return new LampBuilder().name(lamp.name()).bulbs(lamp.bulbs()).shade(lamp.shade()); } // in use: copy a lamp with two bulbs Lamp brighter = toBuilder(new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null)).bulbs(2).build();

steps.say: The function first: its name, a receiver and the return type. The receiver makes it an extension function, which Java doesn't have, so the Java twin is a static method that takes the lamp as a parameter.
steps.code: // 1. the function: name, receiver, return type val toBuilder = FunSpec.builder("toBuilder") .receiver(cls.toClassName()) .returns(builder)

alt.html: // 1. the method: name, modifiers, parameter, return type MethodSpec.Builder toBuilder = MethodSpec.methodBuilder("toBuilder") .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC, Modifier.STATIC) .addParameter(ClassName.get(type), "lamp") .returns(builder);

steps.say: Then the body: one chained call per property. %T writes the builder's type, and %N writes each name, backticks included when a name needs them.
steps.code: // 2. the body: start a builder, then one setter call per property val body = CodeBlock.builder().add("return %T()", builder) for (param in constructorParameters(cls)) { body.add(".%N(%N)", nameOf(param), nameOf(param)) } toBuilder.addCode(body.build())

alt.html: // 2. the body: start a builder, then one setter call per record component CodeBlock.Builder body = CodeBlock.builder().add("return new $T()", builder); for (VariableElement p : params) { String name = p.getSimpleName().toString(); body.add(".$N(lamp.$N())", name, name); } toBuilder.addStatement(body.build());

steps.say: Add it to the file with addFunction(toBuilder.build()) and run. KotlinPoet prints exactly the line from step 1, and brighter comes out as Lamp(name=desk lamp, bulbs=2, shade=null). This works only because every parameter of Lamp is also a property (val), so name can be read back. A plain constructor parameter has nothing to read: that is one more thing a careful processor checks before it writes, the subject of the next lesson.

lab.title: The @Builder processor, written with KotlinPoet
steps: Open BuilderProcessor.kt in labs/ksp/src/main/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l04/ and run the tests first. All five fail with KSP generated no movemate/LampBuilder.kt and the warning l04 not done yet: builderFile: ....

Find and Check are given, in processBuilders: it asks the Resolver, the helper's clipboard that KSP passes to process, for every @Builder symbol and skips anything that isn't a class declaration. Read them; lesson 5 makes Check strict.
Read is given too: constructorParameters(cls) lists the parameters, and inside each spec param.type.toTypeName() turns a type into a KotlinPoet TypeName.

Write, the property: fill in builderProperty so it prints private var name: String? = null. Then the function and its parameter: setterFunction. Then the class: builderType, with the originating file. Then the file: builderFile, with the comment line from its KDoc. buildFunction is given; read how it uses %T, %N and %S.

Prove: run the tests until all five pass. Then run it in the real build with your processor, ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL04Kotlin -Pmine=l04, open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l04/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l04/LampBuilder.kt, and run ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l04.MoveDayKt -Pmine=l04. While your processor is unfinished, use only the kspL04Kotlin task: the app's code calls the builders, so compiling it fails until they exist.
From memory: do the drill below without looking at your code.
hints: PropertySpec.builder(name, type, KModifier.PRIVATE).mutable(true).initializer("null").build(). initializer takes a format string, so "null" prints the word null.
In setterFunction, addParameter(name, type) adds the parameter, returns(builder) the return type, and two addStatement calls the body. Use %N for both names in "this.%N = %N".
If the first test fails on whitespace, compare with the expected text in the test. KotlinPoet adds the blank lines and the two-space indent itself; don't add your own \n.
lab.done: All five tests in BuilderProcessorTest pass, and ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l04.MoveDayKt -Pmine=l04 prints the same six lines as the reference.

drill.title: A property and a setter, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. For a KSValueParameter called param and a builder ClassName called builder, write the KotlinPoet code for the field private var name: String? = null and for the setter public fun name(name: String): LampBuilder, which sets the field and returns the builder. Then write the JavaPoet version for a VariableElement. Which placeholder carries the names, and why?

answer.html: val name = param.name!!.asString() // the field: the parameter's type made nullable, starting empty val field = PropertySpec.builder(name, param.type.toTypeName().copy(nullable = true), KModifier.PRIVATE) .mutable(true) .initializer("null") .build() // the setter: %N for names, so a keyword gets backticks val setter = FunSpec.builder(name) .addParameter(name, param.type.toTypeName()) .returns(builder) .addStatement("this.%N = %N", name, name) .addStatement("return this") .build()

alt.title: JavaPoet
alt.html: String name = param.getSimpleName().toString(); // the field: boxed, so it can start as null FieldSpec field = FieldSpec.builder(TypeName.get(param.asType()).box(), name, Modifier.PRIVATE).build(); // the setter: $N for names MethodSpec setter = MethodSpec.methodBuilder(name) .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC) .addParameter(TypeName.get(param.asType()), name) .returns(builder) .addStatement("this.$N = $N", name, name) .addStatement("return this") .build();

recap: Generated code is ordinary source code, compiled with yours: it needs imports, correct types and legal names. A string template gets them wrong on ordinary classes, and the compiler, not KSP, reports it.

KotlinPoet builds a file from specs (FileSpec, TypeSpec, PropertySpec, FunSpec, ParameterSpec) and format strings with placeholders: %T for types (imported), %N for names (escaped), %S for strings (quoted), %L for literals (as is).

kotlinpoet-ksp converts KSP symbols: toClassName() gets package and nesting right, toTypeName() keeps every ? and type argument, and copy(nullable = true) makes a type nullable without doubling the ?.
addOriginatingKSFile plus writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) hands the file to KSP with the source file it came from; a wrong choice shows only on a later incremental build.
The limit: KotlinPoet models declarations, not expressions, so bodies are still format strings and the compiler is the referee. And KSP can't see default values, so the builder can't fill them in.

explain.prompt: A teammate's processor writes a builder with a string template. It works in their tests, but in the real project the build fails with Unresolved reference 'Box' in the generated file, although Box exists. Explain what is going on and what KotlinPoet would do differently.
explain.answer: The generated builder is an ordinary Kotlin file, and the compiler reads it like any other. It lives in one package and uses Box from another, so it needs an import, and the template never writes imports. Their tests passed because all their test classes sat in one package, where the short name happened to work. The template pastes KSType's display name, which is meant for people, not for another file. With KotlinPoet you pass the type itself, as a TypeName from toTypeName(), through the %T placeholder. KotlinPoet then prints the short name and adds the matching import at the top of the file. The same approach fixes nullable types with copy(nullable = true), nested classes with toClassName(), and keyword names with %N. The compiler still has the last word, so a test should compile the generated file and call it.

deeper.html:
Three more placeholders and behaviours are worth knowing. %P writes a string template: like %S, but it leaves $ alone, so $name stays a template in the generated code. %M writes a member reference from a MemberName, for example MemberName("kotlin.collections", "mutableMapOf"), and adds the import for it. When two types share a simple name, say move.Box and storage.Box in one generated file, KotlinPoet 2.4.0 imports both under aliases (import move.Box as MoveBox) instead of guessing.

Generic classes need one more step. A class such as Shelf<T : Comparable<T>> uses its type parameter in its properties, and KotlinPoet has to know which T is meant. The tool is a TypeParameterResolver, made with toTypeParameterResolver() on the class's type parameters and passed to toTypeName(...). Since 2.4.0 the default resolver also finds type parameters from the enclosing declarations instead of throwing, so older blog posts that say it throws describe an earlier version.

KotlinPoet 2.0 changed how long lines wrap: spaces no longer wrap by default, ♢ marks a space where a line may break, and · is now an ordinary space. Golden-file tests, which compare a whole generated file with a stored copy, will notice such changes across KotlinPoet upgrades. Pair each golden test with one that compiles and calls the generated code, as this lesson's lab does.
